en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Sappāṇakavagga 63.
The Training Rule on Reopening [a Case].
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, knowing that a legal issue had been settled in accordance with the Dhamma, reopened it for a further formal act, saying:
"The act was not done; the act was ill-done; the act must be done again; it was not settled; it was poorly settled; it must be settled again.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant.
“How can the group of six monks, knowing that a legal issue has been settled in accordance with the Dhamma, reopen it for a further formal act? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, monks, that you, knowing that a legal issue has been settled in accordance with the Dhamma, reopen it for a further formal act?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, knowingly reopen for a formal act a legal issue that has been settled in accordance with the Dhamma?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
“Whosoever, a monk, knowingly reopening for a formal legal action that has been settled in accordance with the Dhamma, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Whosoever, moreover:
Whoever is such a one … [as previously described] … a bhikkhu … [as previously described] … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
"Knows" means either he knows by himself, or others inform him, or he informs [others].
"In accordance with the Dhamma" means:
That which is done according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Teacher’s instruction, is called "in accordance with the Dhamma.

A legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) consists of four types of legal issues: a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), a legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), and a legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
"To reopen for re-doing" means:

if one reopens [the matter] thinking, "The legal act was not done; it was badly done; the legal act must be done again; it was not settled; it was poorly settled; it must be settled again," there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If it is a legitimate legal act and one perceives it as a legitimate legal act, yet one reopens it, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If one reopens a legal matter while being in doubt as to whether it is a legal matter, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one reopens a legal matter perceiving it to be an illegal matter, there is no offense.
If one reopens an illegal matter perceiving it to be a legal matter, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as such, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
If one revives [a legal act] while knowing that it was performed contrary to the Dhamma, or by an incomplete assembly, or against one who does not deserve such a legal act—
except for one who is insane or an original offender.
The third training rule concerning reopening [a legal case] is finished.
